dragonsocks:
Hey, kid.
Are your socks
always missing one?

Grown-ups say
the washing machine ate it.

Washing machines don't eat socks.
Washing machines don't even eat dinner.
A dragon took it.
Dragons love collecting socks.

Striped ones, spotted ones,
fuzzy ones.
Ones with a little hole? Those too.

The only socks dragons don't want are Dad's.
Too big.
And a little bit smelly.

Dragons are very polite.
Before they take a sock,
they always ask first.
While you're asleep.
Probably.

A dragon never admits
it took your sock.
It says, “Wasn't me.”

They carry the socks back to their cave
and pile them into a sock mountain.

At night, they burrow in and sleep.
Soft, warm,
and it smells a tiny bit like feet.
Big dragons like long socks.
Little dragons like short socks.

The littlest dragon only wants one,
worn on the tip of its tail.
It says, “This looks the coolest.”

Dragons don't care about left foot or right foot.
One blue sock with one red sock.
They say that's fashion.

So if you want dragons to come over and play,
hang your socks out.
The more, the better.

But there is one thing
you must never, ever forget.

Never give a dragon
a stinky sock.

One sniff of a stinky sock,
and a dragon falls asleep right away.
Standing up? It sleeps standing up.
Upside down? It sleeps anyway.

Sleeping dragons snore
so loud the whole town wobbles.

So keep stinky socks far away.
Farther.
…Okay, right there is good.

On Saturday,
you throw a sock party.

All the dragons come.
Long ones, round ones, flat ones,
and one that keeps saying, “Wasn't me.”

Everyone dances in their socks,
having the best time—

But nobody sees
the puppy bring in a sock.
A sock that played soccer all day.
Sniff—

SNORE! SNORE! SNORE!
The windows rattle, the roof wobbles,
and the puppy jumps into the basket.

Nobody can wake them up.
You take that sock and wash it.
Three times.

Now the sock smells nice.
One by one, the dragons wake up,
yawn, and keep dancing.

Now you know.
Next time a sock goes missing,
don't blame the washing machine.
Go look at the dragon's tail.
It'll say, “Wasn't me.”
dinobubbles:
Hey, kid.
Do you know what dinosaurs love most?
Not roaring.
Not running.
It's bubble baths.

Before a dinosaur gets in the bath,
it always tests the water
with one toe first.
The toe says, “Okay.”
Probably.

Triceratops likes to pile bubbles
on all three horns.
Even in the bath, it wears a hat.

The long-neck needs three bathtubs.
One for its head,
one for its belly,
and one for its tail.
It says, “One part at a time. Extra clean.”

The plates on Stegosaurus's back
are perfect for drying towels.
It says, “My back is a towel rack.”

T. rex's arms are too short
to scrub its back.

It tried a stick.
The stick said, “I quit.”
Snap.

It tried rubbing on a wall.
The wall said, “You're too heavy.”
BOOM.

So if you want dinosaurs to come over,
run a great big tub of bubbles.

The more bubbles,
the faster they come.

But there is one thing
you must never, ever forget.

Never, ever put in
a rubber duck that squeaks.

Dinosaurs aren't afraid of anything.
Not thunder, not the dark.
A shot at the doctor's? It says, “Go ahead.”

Except that one sound…
SQUEAK.

When a dinosaur hears it,
it jumps in fright.
One jump—as high as three houses!

So put the rubber duck
somewhere else.
Up high.
Higher.

On Saturday night,
you throw a bubble bath party.

All the dinosaurs come.
The bathtub says, “It's a little crowded.”
A lot more than a little.

Everyone soaks with their eyes half closed.
So cozy.

But nobody notices
that under the bubbles,
a little rubber duck is floating.
T. rex leans back—
SQUEAK!

All the dinosaurs jump!
Bubbles fly out the window, fill the living room,
and pile up to the ceiling.

You feel around in the bubbles
and find that rubber duck.
Into the drawer. Shut tight.
Click.

Then you get a long, long brush
and scrub T. rex's back.
It says, “A little to the left.”

The bubbles slowly settle down.
Everyone falls asleep.

Now you know:
dinosaurs love bubble baths, are scared of squeaky ducks,
and not one of them can reach its own back.
Tonight at bath time, take a look—
is there a little dinosaur in your bubbles?
dinowantsplay:
Hey, kid.
Do you know what a dinosaur wants most
when it wakes up?
Someone to play with.

Dinosaurs have a funny way
of making friends.

First, they sniff you with their big noses.
SNIIIFF—
Mmm. Smells like a friend.

Then they wag their tails.
One wag means “Hello.”
The flowerpot behind them? Not so lucky.

Last, they give you
their very favorite rock.

The more they like you,
the bigger the rock.

So if one day
your front door is piled high with big rocks,
don't be mad.
It means a dinosaur likes you.

When T. rex asks, “Can I play too?”
it's much too loud.

All the leaves blow right off the tree.
The tree shivers: “Brrr. I'm cold.”
T. rex whispers, “Sorry.”

When Triceratops goes down the slide,
its horns get stuck.

So it's the best at waiting in line.
It never pushes.
Not even once.

The long-neck's neck
is everybody's slide.
One at a time.

But there is one thing
you must never, ever forget.

Never say “No!” to a dinosaur
and then just walk away.

When a dinosaur hears “No,”
it curls up its tail,
tucks in its head—

and turns into a big rock.
Nobody can move it.
Nobody can wake it up.

On Sunday, you're in the backyard
building a dinosaur castle out of blocks.

You're on the most important part.
Gentle hands.
You're even holding your breath.

Little Triceratops walks over,
holding its very favorite rock.
“I want to play too.”

You're in a hurry,
and your mouth goes faster than your brain—
“NO!”
Little Triceratops curls up—

and turns into a big rock,
right in front of the castle door.

The other dinosaurs come over and take one look—
and curl up into rocks too.
One, two, ten…

You push. It won't budge.
“Come on, get up!”
The rock doesn't answer.

You sit on the rock and think and think.
Then you remember:
dinosaurs can't stand “No,”
but they understand “Wait a minute.”

You crouch down and say softly,
“Sorry, I was in the middle of building.
Wait a minute. Almost done.
After this block, you can build the roof. Okay?”

CRACK!
The rock splits open,
and out pops Little Triceratops.

One by one, the other rocks crack open too.
Everyone builds together,
and the castle gets three times bigger.

Little Triceratops builds the roof.
It's a little crooked.
Exactly the right amount of crooked.

Now you know:
when someone wants to play with you, don't say “No.”
Say “Wait a minute. Almost done,”
and then give them something to do.
Oh—and that rock Little Triceratops gave you?
Keep it somewhere safe.
trexwontstop:
Hey, kid.
Do you know what T. rex hates most?

Not rain.
It stands in the rain
and doesn't even move.

Not mosquitoes.
A mosquito lands on its nose,
and it makes a new friend.

Not even hair washing.
It wears the bubbles on its head
like a hat.

It's—
stopping.

Once it starts playing,
it can't stop.
Running? Can't stop.

Hide-and-seek?
Can't stop.
It hides so long, it forgets it's hiding.

Building a rock castle?
From morning till dark,
and it still can't stop.
The moon says, “Even I'm sleepy.”

But there is one thing
that makes it stop, no matter what.
Its tummy starts talking.

Inside every dinosaur's tummy
lives a little drummer.
There's one in your tummy too.

Boom, boom, boom.
That means:
time to go to the bathroom.

When Triceratops hears it,
it goes right away.
It says, “I'll play when I get back.
Same fun.”

The long-neck's tummy
is very far from its head.
Boom, boom, boom takes a long, long time
to get all the way up there.

So it always
sets off before the sun comes up.

Stegosaurus has the hardest time.
The plates on its back
get stuck in the door frame.

But there is one thing
you must never, ever forget:
never keep the little drummer waiting.

If you ignore it,
it drums louder and louder.
Boom, boom, boom turns into BOOM, BOOM, BOOM.

In the end,
it gets tired and stops drumming.
That is not a good thing.

That day, you and T. rex
have a rock-tower contest.
Whoever builds higher wins.

Boom, boom, boom.
T. rex says, “Wait. Let me play a little longer.”
The little drummer says, “Okay.”

Boom, boom, boom, boom!
“Wait a little more, I'm almost winning!”
The little drummer says, “I'm counting to three.”

Boom, boom, boom, boom, boom!
“Just… just a little more…”
You point far away: “The bathroom's over there!”
BOOM! BOOM! BOOM!

T. rex squeezes its knees together
and runs.
The bathroom is more important than winning.
The bathroom is on the other side of the hill!
Across a little river.
Over three stepping stones.

And through a cave.
You run ahead to clear the way.

Almost there… almost there…
The one in the doorway still hasn't moved!

Stegosaurus squeezes out.
Plop! T. rex sits down.
T. rex says, “That was close.”

When they come back, the rock towers are still there.
Not one rock has fallen.
“So if you go right away,
you don't miss any playing at all.”

Now you know:
when your little drummer drums, go right away.
The game will wait for you.
By the way—
is your little drummer knocking right now?
dinojoin:
Hey, kid.
When dinosaurs play a game,
they have a secret password.

If you don't know the password,
you can't get in.

Today, I'll tell you the secret.
Come a little closer.

Closer.
…Okay, that's too close.

But first, you have to hear the whole story.
Then the password is yours.

The dinosaurs' favorite game
is called Roll the Big Egg.
A stone egg bigger than a house.

The egg rolls,
and everybody runs after it.

Triceratops does the pushing.
It pushes so hard, it gets all sweaty.

The long-neck watches the path up front.
It stands the tallest, so it sees the farthest.

The littlest dinosaur shouts “One, two, three!”
But it can only count to two.

So every time, it's:
“One, two… TWO!”
And everybody just stands there, waiting.

Every dinosaur has a job.
So if you want to join,
just saying “I want to play” isn't enough.

The password has two parts.
Part one:
“Can I play too?”

Part two:
“I can help by…”
and then say what you can do.

But there is one thing
you must never, ever forget:
never skip the password
and run in and grab the egg.

The dinosaurs will think you came to steal the egg.
WHOOSH—they all run away.
All that's left is footprints.

One day, from the bottom of the hill,
you see the dinosaurs rolling the big egg.
You feel all wiggly inside.

You want to play SO much, you just run.
The password?
Forgot it.

You rush right over
and throw your arms around the egg.

WHOOSH—
the dinosaurs all run away.

All that's left is a ring of footprints…
and you.

With nobody holding it,
the big stone egg wobbles…
and starts to roll down the hill.

Faster and faster.
It can't stop.

You chase after it.
Your legs get tired.
You can't catch it.

It rolls across the creek, across the meadow.
Up ahead is a big mud puddle.
One more roll, and it's taking a mud bath.

You stop and catch your breath.
Then you remember:
the password.

You turn to the bushes and shout,
“Can I play too?
I can help by stopping the egg!”

The bushes rustle.
Out pops a head.
Then another.

Out rush the dinosaurs!
Triceratops pushes, the long-neck watches the path,
and you stand in front of the mud, hands out—
got it!
Phew. That was close.

The littlest dinosaur stands on a rock and shouts,
“One, two… THREE!”
Now it can count to three.

Now you know the password:
walk over, ask,
and say how you can help.
If they say “Wait a minute,”
the game is only halfway done.
Wait a little. They'll call you.
trexloses:
Hey, kid.
Have you ever played a game with a T. rex?

Whatever T. rex plays,
it wants to win.
Races? It wants to win.
Hide-and-seek? It wants to win.

Even a staring contest?
It wants to win.
Its secret:
it pretends to be a rock.

But T. rex's arms are too short.
When it gets an itch, it needs a friend to scratch it.

Playing catch? It can't catch.
Its secret move: catching with its head.
Jump rope? It can't reach the rope.
So it loses. A lot.

When T. rex loses,
it plops down on its bottom.
THUMP! The cups on the table jump.
It thinks the harder it sits,
the closer it gets to winning.

Lose twice,
and all the apples fall off the tree.

Lose three times…
you really don't want to know.
So everyone lets it win.

Triceratops pretends to trip.
But first, it peeks at T. rex.
The long-neck pretends to fall asleep.

T. rex wins.
But it isn't happy at all.

Because nobody wants
to play with it anymore.

But there is one thing
you must never, ever forget:
never race a T. rex.

You'll win.
And then you'll be in trouble.

One day, you and T. rex
have a race.

You run faster.
You get there first.

T. rex stops.
Its face gets redder… and redder…
It's thinking, “This time, I'll sit down even harder.”

It starts to sit down—
everybody grabs on tight.
THUMP!!!

Everyone bounces into the air.
When the shaking stops,
everyone's hair is standing straight up.

You walk over
and sit down next to it.

You say,
“It's okay to lose.
Let's play again.”
“This time, you count one, two, three.”

Another round.
This time, T. rex wins.

Another round.
This time, you win.
T. rex thinks for a moment,
then sits down slowly.
Gently.
The butterfly on the flower doesn't even fly away.

Soon, everyone comes back.
Whoever loses
gets to count one, two, three for the next race.

Everyone races all afternoon.
Who won?
Nobody remembers.

Now you know:
“It's okay to lose. Let's play again.”
Oh, and if one day
the cups in your house jump—
go take a look.
Maybe somebody lost.
dinoschool:
Hey, kid.
Do you know what a dinosaur is most scared of
on the first day of school?

Not the teacher.
The teacher is a very gentle
long-neck.

Not the classroom.
The classroom has more blocks
than kids.

It's—
saying goodbye to Mom.

Little Triceratops hugs Mom's tail,
tight, tight, tight.
It thinks, “One more minute of hugging.
Just one minute.”

When Mom takes one step,
it slides one step right along with her.

It has a great idea:
bring the house to school.

The next day,
it brings its pillow.

On the third day,
it brings its bed.

On the fourth day, it brings the couch, the lamp,
and the fish tank from home.
All of it.

The classroom is stuffed full.
The teacher's head
can't squeeze in through the window.
Only a nose gets in.

But there is one thing
you must never, ever forget:
never let a dinosaur
bring its whole house to school.

A house is too big to fit in a school.
And anyway, home waits for you.
Look—the light at home is still on.

That day, you're in the same class.
Your chair is behind the fish tank.

You see Little Triceratops
sitting between the couch and the lamp,
all alone, eyes a little red.
It misses Mom.

You remember
that on your first day of school,
you felt like that too.

You walk over and say,
“Can I play with you?”
“I can help you build a castle.”

Little Triceratops thinks about it.
“Okay. A castle sounds good.”
It lets go of its pillow.

You build a castle out of blocks.
Taller than the pillow.

The couch is the castle wall.
The couch is so heavy,
you push till you're all sweaty.

The lamp is the lighthouse.
Now nobody's scared of the dark.

The fish tank is the moat.
The fish is very pleased.

The other little dinosaurs come too.
They line up to take a look.

All of a sudden,
the classroom is full of fun.
Even the fish in the tank
swims faster.

The home-time bell rings.
The castle isn't even finished.

Little Triceratops runs to the door—
faster than anybody.

Mom is right at the door.
She didn't go away. Not one step.

The next day,
Little Triceratops doesn't bring the couch.
It runs even faster than yesterday.

It brings just one
little stone from Mom,
tucked in its pocket.
Nobody else knows.

Whenever it misses Mom,
it gives the stone a little touch.

Now you know:
you don't need to bring your house to school.
Bring one little thing,
make one new friend.
At home time, Mom will be right at the door.
dragonturns:
Hey, kid.
There's a swing in the park.
Just one.
Today, seven dragons show up.

Seven dragons.
One swing.
The swing is getting nervous.
Guess what happens?

Dragons love swinging.
Up high,
wind in their whiskers—it's the best.

But dragons aren't very good at waiting in line.
Every dragon wants to be first.

The long flat dragon starts at the very back.
ZIIIP—
it slips all the way to the front.

The round dragon
sits on the swing and won't get off.
It says, “This swing is round. Just like me.”

The tall skinny dragon waits at the very back
so long that its neck
gets even longer.

The littlest dragon counts:
six dragons in front.
Before it gets dark?
No way it gets a turn.

But there is one thing
you must never, ever forget:
never let seven dragons
sit on one swing at the same time.
The swing will fly all the way to the moon.
One day, you come to the park too.

You see seven dragons squished in a heap.
Every dragon is thinking, “Me first.”

You say,
“I have an idea.”

“Let's make a line.
Everyone gets ten swings,
then it's the next dragon's turn.”

The dragons all say okay.
The long flat dragon says, “I'm the fastest counter.”

The first dragon counts,
“One, two, five, nine, TEN!”

The other dragons say,
“You skipped a bunch!”

The second dragon counts,
“One…”
“One…”
“One…”
and falls asleep counting.

Too slow.
The dragons in line are falling asleep too.

The third dragon counts to ten,
then starts over at one.
And giggles.

Everybody is fed up.
Even the swing is sleepy from waiting.

You say,
“Then let's all count together.”

Everyone gathers around the swing
and counts together:
“One, two, three, four…”

“…eight, nine, TEN!
Next!”

This way, nobody can go too fast,
and nobody can go too slow.

It's the littlest dragon's turn.
It says, “I waited all day!”
Everyone pushes together,
up, up, up.

It isn't even dark yet,
and every dragon has had three turns.

The very last turn is yours.
The seven dragons say, “Hold on tight.”
Then they all push you together.

Now you know:
one swing and seven dragons
can still have lots of fun.
Make a line, ten swings each,
and count together.
You try it too.
seesaw:
Hey, kid.
Do you know what dinosaurs love most
on the playground?
Not the slide.

Not the swings, either.
Dinosaur bottoms are too big to fit.
It's the seesaw.

On a seesaw,
both sides should weigh about the same.

When T. rex sits down—
WHOOSH!
Little Triceratops flies up to snack on the clouds.
It snacks all day long.

When the long-necks sit down,
the seesaw bumps on the ground,
but their heads are still up in the clouds, chatting.

Stegosaurus is the most trouble.
Its back plates get stuck—feet up in the air.
It says, “I'm not stuck. I'm looking at the sky.”

On the playground,
there's also a little T. rex.
Its arms are too short.

Short arms are fine.
The trouble is, when it gets in a hurry,
its mouth sticks shut, like it's full of glue,
and not one word comes out.

It wants a turn on the seesaw—
SMACK! A slap.

It wants to switch—
SMACK! Another slap.

It wants to say “Wait for me!”—
SMACK, SMACK! Right on the tail.

But there is one thing
you must never, ever forget:
never slap back.

Then Triceratops slaps,
Stegosaurus slaps,
and the long-neck slaps with a swish of its tail.

SMACK-SMACK-SMACK-SMACK-SMACK!
The seesaw flips over.
Everybody lands in the sandbox.

Who slapped first?
Nobody remembers.
They only remember that everything hurts.

One day, you and Little Triceratops are on the seesaw.
Squeak—up,
squeak—down.

The little T. rex runs over.
It really wants to play.
Its mouth is glued shut again.

SMACK!
Right on your arm.
That hurt.

You want to slap it back.
Your hand is already up.

But then you remember the sandbox.
You plant both feet.
Your hand that was up goes a new way:
straight out, palm forward—

And you say the magic words, loud:
“STOP!
I don't like that.”

So loud!
The birds in the tree freeze.
Even the wind stops to listen.
The little T. rex freezes, one foot in the air.

You turn and walk two steps away
to find a helper.
The helper is the long-neck teacher.

Teacher bends way down, like a big crane.
You say,
“Teacher, the little T. rex slapped me.
I don't like it.”

Teacher is the tallest one here,
so Teacher sees everything on the playground.
Teacher says, “You said that very clearly.
I heard you.”

Teacher looks down and asks the little T. rex,
“You wanted to play. So why did you use your hands?”
The little T. rex says quietly,
“I wanted to play too.
But my mouth got glued shut.”

Teacher says, “When you want to play,
peel off the glue and use your words.”
The little T. rex says, “I'm sorry.
Can I play too?”
You say, “Yes.”

You all play on the seesaw together.
The little T. rex sits down—
and up you fly, so high,
even higher than Little Triceratops.
Everybody laughs.

Now you know:
when you want to play, say it—don't use your hands.
If someone slaps you, don't slap back.
Put out your hand and say the magic words:
“STOP! I don't like that.”
Then walk away and go find a teacher.
After that, you can still be friends.
rafflesia:
Today I'm going into the forest to find a flower.
They say it's the biggest flower in the world.
Bigger than my face.

The forest is very quiet.
There's a big green elephant, standing very still.
It's pretending to be a leaf.

A thick vine is climbing up a tree,
round and round, wrapping the trunk as it climbs.
It looks like a big snake.
But it's a vine, not a snake.

A round bump is swelling up on the vine,
like a great big cabbage.

I sit down and wait.
I wait, and wait.
Then suddenly—crack!

It's blooming!
Five thick petals, bright red, covered in white spots.
It's bigger than my head,
so I wear it on my head like a hat.

But… it's so stinky!
So stinky, the flies all come for a meeting.

That's strange. Where are this flower's leaves?
Where are its roots?
Did it forget to bring them?

It turns out it has no leaves and no roots.
It lives inside the vine's tummy,
drinking the vine's water and eating the vine's dinner.
That's called being a “parasite.”

Other flowers sit in the sun and make their own food.
This one eats at somebody else's house.
It never cooks—and it still grows the biggest flower in the world.
ants:
The sun is out, so I run into the yard to play.
Huh? There's a thin black line on the ground.
And it's moving!
I crouch down and creep closer.

It isn't a line at all—
it's lots and lots of ants,
one behind the other, marching in a row.
They line up even better than I do.

Every single one is carrying something.
A grain of rice, a cookie crumb, a tiny piece of leaf.
The littlest ant
is carrying something bigger than itself.
Dad says ants are super strong.

They carry the dirt out one grain at a time
and pile it into a tiny hill by the door.
When one trip is done, they go back for another.
I count to ten… and then I lose count.

Two ants meet
and touch the little feelers on their heads.
“Hello!”
“There's yummy food over there!”
They don't talk with their mouths.
They talk with their feelers.

I follow the line to a tiny hole.
The ants go in one after another,
like they're going home.
How do they know the way?
The ants in front leave a smell behind, and the ones in back follow it.
I sniff too. I can't smell a thing.

Huh—the sky suddenly gets dark.
The wind comes, and the grass goes swish, swish.
My hair starts dancing in the wind.

Mom calls from the door, “It's going to rain! Come inside!”
The ants are hurrying home too.
They're even faster than me.
Mom says when the air gets damp,
ants know that rain is coming.
They know before I do.

Their home has lots of doors,
hidden in the grass and under the rocks.
Mom says one ant home
has tens of thousands of ants living in it.
Under the ground, there's a whole big city.

Drip, drop.
It's raining.
I hide under my umbrella,
and the ants hide in their home.
We can all hear the rain.
dino:
At the museum, there's a great big dinosaur.
Only its bones are left.
I want to ask it,
“Where did you all go?”

A long, long time ago,
there were dinosaurs all over the Earth.
There were no people yet,
and no me, either.

Some dinosaurs were taller than a house,
with necks long enough to reach the treetops.
But some were only about as big as a chicken.

Huh? This little dinosaur
is wearing a fluffy coat.
Just like a baby chick.

One day, a huge rock fell out of the sky.
It was bigger than a mountain.

BOOM—
The sky went dark.
The sun hid away.
It was so cold.

One by one, the big dinosaurs disappeared.
But some small, feathered dinosaurs
hid in holes and survived.

The sun came back out.
The little dinosaurs' children, and their children's children,
grew longer and longer feathers,
and one day, they flew.

They became—birds!
Birds are the dinosaurs' children.
The dinosaurs didn't go far.
They've been here all along.

I put some bread crumbs out in the yard.
The sparrows fly down to eat.
I whisper,
“Hello, little dinosaurs.”
sea:
It's my first time at the beach.
The sea is so big, I can't see the end of it.
The waves go rumble, rumble.
I hold Dad's hand tight.

Dad says,
“We won't go in the water.
We'll just sit here and watch.”
The sand is warm,
like a blanket that's been out in the sun.

Here comes a wave—
it touches my feet!
I jump.
But it stops,
and then it goes back.

Here it comes again.
It stops in the same place.
Every time,
it stops in the very same spot.

I count: one, two, three…
and the wave comes in.
One, two, three…
and the wave goes out.
So it has a beat,
like it's dancing.

When the wave goes back,
it leaves presents on the sand:
a white seashell,
a piece of seaweed,
and a tiny little hole.

Between the rocks there are little puddles.
They're a little bit of sea
the waves forgot to take with them
when they left.
It's called a “tide pool.”

Lots of little creatures live inside:
a tiny crab, walking sideways,
a little fish, shorter than my finger,
and a starfish,
crawling slowly, slowly.

They aren't scared at all.
They're waiting for the next wave
to come and take them home.

I stand up and walk over slowly.
A wave comes in and touches my feet.
It's cool and tickly.
Then it goes back out.
I say, “I'll come back tomorrow.”
crab:
It's the same beach.
Today I'm brave enough to go a little closer.
I squat down to look for shells.
I'm looking for one that runs.

I pick up a pretty shell.
Huh—it's moving!
It grows legs and runs away!

Dad says,
“That's not a shell.
It's a hermit crab.
It lives in somebody else's empty shell.”

A hermit crab doesn't have a hard shell of its own.
The front of it is hard,
but the back is soft and curly.
So it finds an empty shell,
crawls inside, and carries it around.
Wherever it goes, its house goes too.

I put it back on the sand.
It carries its house on its back
and slowly walks away,
leaving a trail of tiny footprints.

But it keeps on growing.
The shell doesn't grow with it.
One day,
its bottom sticks out!

So it has to move.
It tries one—too small.
It tries another—too big.
It tries one more—just right!

It zips out of the old shell
and into the new one, quick as a wink.
For that one second,
its bottom is bare.
That's when it feels the most nervous.

Sometimes
a bunch of hermit crabs line up.
The big one moves into a new shell
and leaves its old one for a smaller crab.
One passes to the next, and everybody gets a house.

I take the empty shells I found
and put them back on the beach.
Maybe there's a hermit crab
looking for a house right now.
